r.name: ġēr
r.note: Also written ᛡ in inscriptions; manuscripts give ᛡ the separate name īor (see below).
poem:
Ger byþ gumena hiht, ðonne God læteþ,
halig heofones cyning, hrusan syllan
beorhte bleda beornum ond ðearfum.
Harvest is men’s hope, when God, the holy king of heaven, lets the earth give bright fruits to rich and needy.

r.name: ēoh
poem:
Eoh byþ utan unsmeþe treow,
heard hrusan fæst, hyrde fyres,
wyrtrumun underwreþyd, wyn on eþle.
The yew is a tree rough on the outside, hard and fast in the earth, keeper of fire, propped by its roots, a joy on an estate.

r.name: peorð
r.note: The meaning of the name is unknown; the poem only says it brings “play and laughter”.
poem:
Peorð byþ symble plega and hlehter
wlancum [on middum], ðar wigan sittaþ
on beorsele bliþe ætsomne.
Peorð is always play and laughter for the proud, where warriors sit happily together in the beer-hall.

s: the rune eolh: unknown, perhaps “elk” (the poem says eolh-secg “elk-sedge”)

r.name: eolh
r.sound: none: used only to write Latin x
poem:
Eolh-secg eard hæfþ oftust on fenne
wexeð on wature, wundaþ grimme,
blode breneð beorna gehwylcne
ðe him ænigne onfeng gedeþ.
Elk-sedge usually lives in the fen; it grows in water and wounds grimly, burning with blood any man who grabs it.

logo.t: In one manuscript (Corpus Christi College, MS 41) a writer seems to use runes like Roman numerals: ᛉᛁᛁ⁊ᛉᛉᛉᛋᚹᛁᚦᚩᚱ, which likely means “12 & 30 more”, with ᛉ as ten and ᛁ as one.

r.name: siġel
poem:
Sigel semannum symble biþ on hihte,
ðonne hi hine feriaþ ofer fisces beþ,
oþ hi brimhengest bringeþ to lande.
The sun is always a hope to sailors as they cross the fish’s bath, until the sea-horse (the ship) brings them to land.

s: the rune tīr: unknown: tīr “glory”, or the god Tīw

r.name: tīr
poem:
Tir biþ tacna sum, healdeð trywa wel
wiþ æþelingas; a biþ on færylde
ofer nihta genipu, næfre swiceþ.
Tir is a sign; it keeps faith well with princes; it is always on its course over the mists of night and never fails.

r.name: beorc
poem:
Beorc byþ bleda leas, bereþ efne swa ðeah
tanas butan tudder, biþ on telgum wlitig,
heah on helme hrysted fægere,
geloden leafum, lyfte getenge.
The birch has no fruit, yet bears shoots without seed; it is lovely in its branches, high in its crown, beautifully adorned, laden with leaves, touching the sky.

r.name: eh
poem:
Eh byþ for eorlum æþelinga wyn,
hors hofum wlanc, ðær him hæleþ ymb[e]
welege on wicgum wrixlaþ spræce
and biþ unstyllum æfre frofur.
The horse is the joy of princes among warriors, a steed proud of its hooves, when wealthy riders trade talk about it; and to the restless it is always a comfort.

logo.t: One of the runes in Cynewulf’s runic signature. In The Fates of the Apostles, Juliana, Elene and Christ II the letters of his name (C-Y-N-(E)-W-U-L-F) are woven into the verse as runes that also stand for words fitting the passage.

r.name: mann
r.note: Used in manuscripts as a shorthand for the word mann.
poem:
Man byþ on myrgþe his magan leof:
sceal þeah anra gehwylc oðrum swican,
forðum drihten wyle dome sine
þæt earme flæsc eorþan betæcan.
A man in his joy is dear to his kinsman; yet each must fail the other, for the Lord by his decree will hand that poor flesh to the earth.

logo.t: Written for the word mann “man” in manuscripts such as the Beowulf manuscript (Nowell Codex) and the Exeter Book.
Birkett lists mon among the runes “used on occasion” as abbreviations in Anglo-Saxon manuscripts.

s: the rune lagu: water, sea, lake

r.name: lagu
poem:
Lagu byþ leodum langsum geþuht,
gif hi sculun neþan on nacan tealtum
and hi sæyþa swyþe bregaþ
and se brimhengest bridles ne gym[eð].
Water seems endless to people when they must venture out in a rocking ship, the sea-waves terrify them, and the sea-horse ignores its bridle.

logo.t: One of the runes in Cynewulf’s runic signature. In The Fates of the Apostles, Juliana, Elene and Christ II the letters of his name (C-Y-N-(E)-W-U-L-F) are woven into the verse as runes that also stand for words fitting the passage.

s: the rune ing: Ing, a hero or god (perhaps Ingui-Frea)

r.name: ing
r.mean: Ing, a hero or god (perhaps Ingui-Frea)
poem:
Ing wæs ærest mid East-Denum
gesewen secgun, oþ he siððan est
ofer wæg gewat; wæn æfter ran;
ðus Heardingas ðone hæle nemdun.
Ing was first seen by men among the East-Danes, until he later went away over the waves, with his wagon running after; so the Heardings named the hero.

s: the rune ēþel: inherited land, homeland

r.name: ēþel
r.note: Used in the Beowulf manuscript as shorthand for the word ēþel.
poem:
Eþel byþ oferleof æghwylcum men,
gif he mot ðær rihtes and gerysena on
brucan on bolde bleadum oftast.
Home is very dear to every man, if there in his house he may enjoy what is right and fitting, with plenty most of the time.

logo.t: Written for the word ēþel “homeland” in the Beowulf manuscript (British Library, Cotton Vitellius A XV, fol. 141v): þǫnǫn hé ge·sóhte · swę́sne ᛟ, “from there he sought out his beloved [homeland]”.

r.name: dæġ
poem:
Dæg byþ drihtnes sond, deore mannum,
mære metodes leoht, myrgþ and tohiht
eadgum and earmum, eallum brice.
Day is the Lord’s messenger, dear to men, the Creator’s glorious light, joy and hope to rich and poor, useful to all.

logo.t: Birkett lists dæg among the runes “used on occasion” as abbreviations for their names in Anglo-Saxon manuscripts.

r.name: āc
r.note: New Anglo-Frisian rune, split from Elder ᚨ; earliest examples 6th century.
poem:
Ac byþ on eorþan elda bearnum
flæsces fodor, fereþ gelome
ofer ganotes bæþ; garsecg fandaþ
hwæþer ac hæbbe æþele treowe.
On land the oak feeds the flesh (of pigs) for the children of men; often it travels over the gannet’s bath (as a ship), and the ocean tests whether the oak keeps noble faith.

r.name: æsċ
r.note: New Anglo-Frisian rune, split from Elder ᚨ.
poem:
Æsc biþ oferheah, eldum dyre
stiþ on staþule, stede rihte hylt,
ðeah him feohtan on firas monige.
The ash is very tall and dear to men, sturdy on its base; it holds its ground rightly though many men fight against it.

r.name: ȳr
r.note: English addition with no Elder ancestor; the name may just be modelled on ūr.
poem:
Yr byþ æþelinga and eorla gehwæs
wyn and wyrþmynd, byþ on wicge fæger,
fæstlic on færelde, fyrdgeatewa sum.
Ȳr is a joy and an honour to every prince and nobleman; it looks fine on horseback and is reliable on a journey, a piece of war-gear.

logo.t: One of the runes in Cynewulf’s runic signature. In The Fates of the Apostles, Juliana, Elene and Christ II the letters of his name (C-Y-N-(E)-W-U-L-F) are woven into the verse as runes that also stand for words fitting the passage.

s: the rune īor: unknown, perhaps “beaver” or “eel”; the poem calls it a river-fish that feeds on land

r.name: īor
r.mean: unknown, perhaps “beaver” or “eel”; the poem calls it a river-fish that feeds on land
r.note: Page called it a pseudo-rune: in inscriptions ᛡ is only a variant of ġēr.
poem:
Iar byþ eafix and ðeah a bruceþ
fodres on foldan, hafaþ fægerne eard
wætre beworpen, ðær he wynnum leofaþ.
Īor is a river-fish, yet always takes its food on land; it has a fair home ringed with water, where it lives in delight.

s: the rune ēar: unknown, perhaps “earth” (the dictionary’s ēar means “wave” or “ear of grain”)

r.name: ēar
r.mean: unknown, perhaps “earth” (the dictionary’s ēar means “wave” or “ear of grain”)
r.note: English addition with no Elder ancestor.
poem:
Ear byþ egle eorla gehwylcun,
ðonn[e] fæstlice flæsc onginneþ,
hraw colian, hrusan ceosan
blac to gebeddan; bleda gedreosaþ,
wynna gewitaþ, wera geswicaþ.
Ēar is hateful to every nobleman, when the flesh, the corpse, steadily begins to grow cold and, pale, to choose the earth as its bedfellow; fruits fall, joys pass away, promises fail.

s: the rune calc: chalk? chalice? sandal?

r.name: calc
r.note: Ruthwell Cross, Bramham Moor ring, Kingmoor ring and manuscripts. A Northumbrian-era addition, made from ċēn to separate hard /k/ from palatalized c.

r.name: gār
r.note: Ruthwell Cross, probably Bewcastle Cross, and manuscripts. Made from ġyfu to separate hard /g/ from palatalized g.

r.name: cweorð
r.note: Manuscripts only. Page thought it pointless, perhaps invented just to match Latin Q.

r.name: (no name)
r.note: Found only on the Ruthwell Cross, where it seems to replace calc before a fronted vowel.
